summary: Describes the interim NETRJS remote job entry service for the UCLA Campus Computing Network IBM 360 Model 91. Rand and UCLA/NMC had written user programs for it. It replaced RFC 88 and was expected to be superseded by a revised version. It was replaced by RFC 599.

plainLanguage.summary: NETRJS let a remote user submit card-image jobs to UCLA's batch system and collect the resulting print or punch output. This RFC describes an interim version of the service and its separate console and data connections.

subtitle: An interim protocol for remote job entry to UCLA's IBM 360 Model 91.

tldr.problem: Remote ARPANET users needed to submit batch jobs to the UCLA Campus Computing Network and receive their output.
tldr.mechanism: A user process acts as a virtual remote batch terminal, using a Telnet console connection and separate data channels for card-reader input, printer output, and punch output.
tldr.outcome: This is an interim specification, later obsoleted by RFC 599 and updated by RFC 283.

today: RFC 189 is an interim NETRJS specification that obsoletes RFC 88. It was later obsoleted by RFC 599 and updated by RFC 283.

sections.title: Remote Job Entry to UCLA
sections.content:
NETRJS gave remote users access to the Remote Job Service on the UCLA Campus Computing Network's 360 Model 91. Each active user process appeared to the service as a virtual remote batch terminal (VRBT), with virtual card-reader, printer, and punch devices.

Users sent card images containing jobs to the batch system. Print and punch output returned to the originating VRBT unless the job's JCL specified another destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote computer could act as a virtual terminal for UCLA's batch service. The user sent jobs through a virtual card reader and received output through a virtual printer or punch.

sections.title: Sessions and Separate Channels
sections.content:
The user started a session with the standard Initial Connection Protocol to an ASCII or EBCDIC socket at CCN. The connection established a duplex Telnet operator console; the user then signed on with a terminal ID.

Data-transfer channels were separate from the console and could be opened for input and output. A session ended when the user closed all connections or issued SIGNOFF; after SIGNOFF, RJS waited for current output streams to complete before closing connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The user signed in over a console connection, then opened separate connections for job data and output. Signing off let current output finish before the session closed.

sections.title: Job Input and Output
sections.content:
A submitted job stream consists of card-image records of at most 80 characters. A stack can contain successive jobs, with each new job recognized by a JOB card. The user sends an End-of-Data transaction to start processing the final job in the stack.

Data records are grouped in transactions with a 72-bit header containing a sequence number and data length. CCN buffers are 880 bytes, so one transaction cannot exceed 880 bytes. Output is sent over an open printer or punch channel; the RFC describes compressed and truncated record formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Jobs enter as a sequence of card images, with a JOB card marking each new job. Numbered transactions carry the input and output records over the data channels.

sections.title: Console and Output Controls
sections.content:
The operator console accepts commands for session and job management. STATUS reports jobs associated with the VRBT, while commands such as DEFER and RESET move output between queues, ROUTE changes an output destination, and ABORT cancels a job.

For an output stream, BACKSPACE can repeat an earlier portion and RESTART can repeat from the last SYSOUT data set or the beginning of the job. RJS retains output state so a user can reopen a channel later.
sections.plainLanguage: Console commands let users check job status and manage where output goes. They can also request that interrupted output restart from an earlier point.
